questions.question: What equation is stated by the Fundamental Theorem of Linear Maps?
options: $\dim V+\dim W=\dim(\ker A)$.
$\dim(\ker A)+\dim(\operatorname{range}A)=\dim V$.
$\dim(\operatorname{range}A)=\dim W$ always.
$\ker A=\operatorname{range}A$.

questions.question: Which dimension is split by the rank–nullity theorem?
options: The dimension of the codomain.
The number of equations in the codomain.
The number of scalars in the field.
The dimension of the domain.

questions.question: What is another name for the Fundamental Theorem of Linear Maps?
options: The triangle inequality.
The rank-nullity theorem.
The complex conjugate root theorem.
Cramer’s rule.

questions.question: What does the kernel part of the rank–nullity theorem count?
options: Outputs that fill the codomain.
The number of bases of $W$.
The number of scalar fields.
Domain directions sent to zero.

questions.question: What hypothesis on $V$ appears in the rank–nullity theorem?
options: $V$ must be over $\mathbb C$ only.
$V$ is finite-dimensional.
$V$ must equal $W$.
$V$ is the zero vector space only.

questions.question: If $A:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^2$ has $\dim\ker A=1$, what is $\dim\operatorname{range}A$?
If $\dim V=5$ and $\dim\ker A=2$, what is $\dim\operatorname{range}A$?
If $\dim V=4$ and $\dim\operatorname{range}A=4$, what is $\dim\ker A$?
If $A\in\mathcal L(V)$, $\dim V=3$, and $\ker A=\{0\}$, what is $\dim\operatorname{range}A$?
If $\dim V=6$ and $\dim\operatorname{range}A=2$, what is $\dim\ker A$?
How does the rank–nullity theorem connect injectivity with dimension?
options: Injectivity forces the domain to be infinite-dimensional.
Injectivity is unrelated to the kernel.
Injectivity makes the range dimension zero.
Injectivity gives nullity $0$, so rank equals the domain dimension.

questions.question: How does the rank–nullity theorem connect surjectivity with dimension?
options: Surjectivity gives range $W$, so rank is $\dim W$.
Surjectivity means the range has dimension zero.
Surjectivity means the kernel has dimension zero.
Surjectivity means the kernel is the whole domain.

questions.question: Why are the words “directions lost” and “directions visible” useful here?
options: They say every lost direction reappears unchanged in the range.
They replace the need for a dimension equation.
They mean the map is never injective.
Kernel directions are lost; range directions remain visible.

questions.question: If $A:\mathbb R^4\to\mathbb R^2$ is surjective, what is $\dim\ker A$?
If $A:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^5$ is injective, what is $\dim\operatorname{range}A$?
If $\dim\ker A=3$ and $\dim\operatorname{range}A=4$, what is $\dim V$?
Why can rank-nullity rule out some proposed kernel and range dimensions?
options: They must always be equal to each other.
Their sum must equal the dimension of the domain.
Their product must equal the dimension of the codomain.
They must both be zero.

questions.question: For $A\in\mathcal L(V)$ with $V$ finite-dimensional, why does injectivity imply surjectivity?
options: Injectivity makes the codomain smaller.
Injectivity means every vector maps to zero, no matter which values are selected.
This implication never holds for operators.
Kernel dimension $0$ forces range dimension $\dim V$, so the range is all of $V$.

questions.question: Can a linear map $A:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^2$ be injective?
options: Yes, every map from a larger space to a smaller one is injective.
Yes, because the codomain has fewer coordinates.
No, because all maps to $\mathbb R^2$ have zero range.
No, its range dimension is at most $2$, so rank-nullity gives a nonzero kernel.

questions.question: Is it possible for $A:\mathbb R^4\to\mathbb R^2$ to have $\dim\ker A=1$?
options: Yes, rank-nullity would give range dimension $1$, under all circumstances whatsoever.
No, then the range dimension would be $3$, impossible inside $\mathbb R^2$.
No, because kernels cannot have dimension $1$.
Yes, every kernel dimension is possible.
